summary: A browser tool that lets students and the public pick an Earth-science variable and a place, then find out what is changing, where, how much, and whether the change is statistically significant. It downloads real NASA data on the spot (MERRA-2, CERES and MODIS products through the NASA POWER API, with no account needed) and explains every result in plain language.
details:
Our tool is a free web app that lets anyone pick an Earth science variable and a place on Earth, then tells them what is changing, where, how fast, and whether the change is statistically significant. Users answer three questions: what to investigate (21 variables across heat, water, ice and snow, air, and sun and clouds, each explained in plain language), where (click a point or drag a region on the map), and when (any year range, and optionally a single season or month). The app then downloads real NASA data straight from the NASA POWER API (MERRA-2, CERES and MODIS-derived products), removes the seasonal cycle and runs three tests side by side: Sen’s slope with a 95% confidence interval, the Mann–Kendall test corrected for autocorrelation, and a t-test. The result is a one-sentence verdict, such as “Air temperature at Singapore is rising: +0.22 °C per decade, 3 of 3 tests agree.”

It goes beyond a single trend line. It estimates how many more years of data a weak trend needs before it can be proven. It detects when a trend reversed direction. It maps every grid cell in a region with false-discovery control and flags opposite trends inside one area. It warns when the data itself looks broken. A Trend Scanner tests 20 variables at once so the data suggests what to investigate, and five Case Files walk through real published findings step by step.

Benefits and intended impact
It needs no installation, account or coding, and it runs on a phone or a school laptop. It’s aimed at high school and university students and the interested public, so every number comes with a plain explanation. Teachers can use the Case Files as ready-made lessons. We want people to be able to check climate claims about their own city for themselves, and to understand the difference between a real trend and noise.

Tools and technologies
JavaScript (no framework), HTML and CSS, plotly.js for charts, and an HTML canvas map with Natural Earth coastlines. Data comes from the NASA POWER API. We also wrote a Python reference implementation (NumPy, SciPy), and tested everything with 141 automated checks in Node.js plus browser tests in Playwright. The app is hosted on GitHub Pages.

Creativity
The statistical method was adapted from atomistic simulations of nanoparticle growth and dissolution. Measuring a growth rate from a noisy shape descriptor maps directly onto measuring a climate trend from noisy monthly data. That background also gave us a fix: the standard autocorrelation correction still produced 12–19% false alarms, and summing the autocorrelation only to its first zero crossing, as is done for correlation times in simulations, brought it down to 5–8%.

Factors we considered
Scientific validity came first. We checked the tool against published results using real NASA data: Singapore warming of +0.22 °C/decade against the Met Service’s +0.24, East China aerosols rising +0.107 then falling −0.264 per decade against a published +0.11 and −0.26, and Arctic September sea ice at −10.5% per decade against NSIDC’s −12.1%. We openly report where we disagree: MERRA-2 shows slower Arctic warming than observations. We also designed for readability by non-experts, worked within NASA POWER’s rate limits, and added a data-quality check after finding a real jump in the precipitation record over Singapore after 2021.
